objectives: Determine the steric number of a central atom from its Lewis structure by counting bonding pairs and lone pairs.
Predict the electron-domain geometry of a molecule from its steric number, identifying the linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal, or octahedral arrangement.
Distinguish electron-domain geometry from molecular geometry, and identify the molecular shape produced when one or more domains is a lone pair.
Explain why lone pairs occupy more angular space than bonding pairs, and predict the direction of bond-angle deviations from idealized values.

modules.description: Introduces VSEPR theory and the concept of electron domain repulsion.
modules.author: AI Educational Content Designer
educationalObjectives: Understand the core principle of VSEPR theory: electron pairs arrange to minimize repulsion.
Identify how to count electron domains from a Lewis structure.
instructions: Welcome to the VSEPR Theory lab!
This lab explores how molecules achieve their 3D shapes.
We'll start by understanding the fundamental principle: electron pairs around a central atom repel each other and spread out as much as possible.
In this first scene, you'll see a central atom and learn how to count electron domains from a Lewis structure.

components.text: Electron pairs repel. Molecules adopt shapes that minimize this repulsion.
Rule: Single, double, triple bonds, and lone pairs EACH count as one electron domain.
Electron pairs repel. Molecules adopt shapes that minimize this repulsion.

educationalObjectives: Observe and understand the minimum-repulsion principle in action.

instructions: In this module, we'll see VSEPR theory in action!
Watch as electron domains arrange themselves to be as far apart as possible.
We'll start with two domains, then add a third, and finally a fourth, observing the resulting geometries.

instructions: Now let's explore the geometries for 5 and 6 electron domains.

Observe the trigonal bipyramidal and octahedral shapes.

instructions: Electron domains determine the overall shape, but lone pairs aren't counted as part of the molecular shape.
We'll look at methane (CH4), ammonia (NH3), and water (H2O) to see this distinction.

instructions: Lone pairs push bonding pairs closer together.
See how the bond angles change as lone pairs increase.

modules.description: Summarizes the key concepts covered in the VSEPR theory lab.
modules.author: AI Educational Content Designer
educationalObjectives: Consolidate understanding of VSEPR theory principles.
Review the relationship between Lewis structures and 3D molecular geometry.
instructions: You have successfully explored VSEPR theory!
Let's quickly recap the main concepts you've learned.

components.text: 1. Minimum Repulsion Principle: Electron domains arrange to be as far apart as possible.
2. Electron Domain Geometries: Linear, Trigonal Planar, Tetrahedral, Trigonal Bipyramidal, Octahedral.
3. Molecular vs. Electron Domain Geometry: Lone pairs affect molecular shape but not electron domain geometry.
4. Lone Pair Asymmetry: Lone pairs occupy more space, compressing bond angles.
5. Application: VSEPR predicts the shapes of real molecules.
